learning_goal: Count the airway generations from the bronchial buds to the terminal bronchiole, name the four stages of lung maturation with their weeks, say what tissue change defines each stage, and state the earliest age at which a preterm baby can exchange gas and why.

terms: eight to ten segments on the left

structures.label: Where the branching starts — the two bronchial buds
structures.narration: Branching begins from the two bronchial buds already made by the respiratory diverticulum. Each bud is a blind endodermal tube capped by splanchnic mesoderm, and every airway below it is made by the same trick repeated: the tube divides in two, and the mesenchyme around it tells it where and when.

structures.label: Second generation — the lobar bronchi, three right and two left
structures.narration: In week five each bud divides into secondary buds — three on the right, two on the left. These are the lobar bronchi, and the lobe count of the adult lung is fixed here. The left has two because the heart takes the space where a middle lobe would sit; the lingula is what remains of it.

structures.label: Third generation — segmental bronchi and the bronchopulmonary segments
terms: eight to ten segments on the left
structures.narration: By weeks six and seven the lobar bronchi divide into tertiary buds — ten on the right, eight to ten on the left. Each tertiary bud plus the lung tissue and the mesenchyme around it becomes one bronchopulmonary segment, wrapped in its own connective tissue with its own artery. That independence is why a surgeon can take out one segment and leave the rest of the lobe working.

structures.label: Seventeen generations by birth, twenty-three in the adult
structures.narration: Branching is dichotomous and it does not stop at birth. Seventeen orders of branches exist by the time the baby is born; six more are added afterwards, giving the adult's twenty-three. Learn the boundary rather than the number: everything down to the terminal bronchiole only conducts air, and gas exchange begins at the respiratory bronchiole.

structures.label: What tells the tube to branch — mesenchyme, not endoderm
structures.narration: The endodermal tube does not decide its own pattern. The surrounding splanchnic mesenchyme induces each division, and the endoderm supplies the epithelium that grows into it. Two consequences follow and both are examinable: the same rule as the diverticulum still holds — endoderm inside, splanchnic mesoderm outside — and a lung that has no room to expand cannot branch, so anything that crowds the thorax gives a hypoplastic lung.

structures.label: Pseudoglandular stage — weeks 5 to 16
structures.narration: From week five to sixteen the lung looks like an exocrine gland under the microscope — tubules of thick columnar epithelium in loose mesenchyme, which is what gives the stage its name. All the conducting airways down to the terminal bronchioles are built in this window. Nothing here can exchange gas, so a fetus born in this stage cannot survive whatever is done for it.

structures.label: Canalicular stage — weeks 16 to 26
structures.narration: From sixteen to twenty-six weeks the terminal bronchioles canalise, each dividing into respiratory bronchioles and then alveolar ducts, and capillaries grow in around them while the epithelium thins. This is the stage where the lung first becomes a gas-exchanging organ rather than a branching tree. Towards its end, at about twenty-two to twenty-four weeks, some thin-walled sacs and their capillaries are close enough for a baby to survive with intensive care — this is the limit of viability, and it exists because of vascularisation, not because of branching.

structures.label: Terminal saccular stage — week 26 to birth
structures.narration: From twenty-six weeks to term, many more terminal sacs form and their walls thin to a true blood-air barrier — flat type one pneumocytes against capillary endothelium. Type two pneumocytes appear among them and begin making surfactant, in small amounts from about week twenty and in adequate amounts from about week twenty-six to twenty-eight. Survival after this point is largely a question of how much surfactant there is.

structures.label: Alveolar stage — week 36 to about 8 years
structures.narration: Mature alveoli only start forming at about week thirty-six, and the great majority form after birth — roughly fifty million at term against three hundred million in the adult, with the process running to about eight years of age. Say this in an exam and say it exactly: the newborn lung is not a small adult lung, it is an unfinished one, and it grows by making new alveoli rather than by enlarging old ones.

structures.label: What goes wrong with branching
structures.narration: Branching fails in two ways. It can go wrong in itself: an abnormal overgrowth of terminal bronchiolar tissue gives a cystic adenomatoid malformation, and a bud that pinches off from the airway gives a bronchogenic cyst. Or it can be prevented from outside, and this is the common one — a diaphragmatic hernia filling the chest, or oligohydramnios from renal agenesis, leaves the lung with nowhere to expand and no stimulus to divide, so it stays hypoplastic. In Potter sequence it is the lungs that kill the baby, not the kidneys.

views.title: One tube divides in two, over and over
views.narration: Start with the two bronchial buds. Branching morphogenesis is one move repeated: a blind endodermal tube divides into two, each daughter divides again, and the mesenchyme around it decides where. Nothing new is invented after this point — the whole tree from main bronchus to alveolar duct is this one move, run twenty-three times.

views.title: The first three generations, and why the segments matter
views.narration: Follow one breath down. Main bronchus, then lobar — three right, two left, and the lobe count is settled in week five. Then segmental — ten right, eight to ten left — and each of those, with its mesenchyme and its own artery, becomes a bronchopulmonary segment. Then the count runs on: seventeen generations by birth, twenty-three in the adult, with gas exchange starting at the respiratory bronchiole.

views.title: Mesenchyme instructs, endoderm obeys
views.narration: Lift the mesodermal coat off the tube. The pattern is written in the mesenchyme, not the epithelium — signals from the splanchnic mesoderm tell the endodermal tip when and where to split. The same rule as the lung bud still holds, endoderm inside and splanchnic mesoderm outside, and it carries a clinical corollary: a lung with no space to expand receives no signal to branch.

views.title: Four stages, four weeks to remember
views.narration: Put the four stages side by side and read the weeks off: pseudoglandular five to sixteen, canalicular sixteen to twenty-six, terminal saccular twenty-six to birth, alveolar thirty-six weeks to eight years. Each is named for what the tissue looks like. Gland-like tubules, then canals with capillaries, then thin-walled sacs, then true alveoli. Learn the names as descriptions and the weeks come with them.

views.title: Where viability starts, and why

ops.kind: thin walls and capillaries, then surfactant, make survival possible at

views.narration: The line between a fetus that cannot survive and one that might is drawn late in the canalicular stage. It is not drawn by branching — the conducting airways were finished at sixteen weeks and could not exchange a molecule of gas. It is drawn by capillaries growing up against thinning epithelium, at about twenty-two to twenty-four weeks. Surfactant then decides how well: enough of it by twenty-six to twenty-eight weeks, and a preterm baby has a real chance.

views.title: Branching that goes wrong, and branching that is prevented

ops.kind: no space to expand, therefore no signal to divide, giving

views.narration: Two groups. Disordered branching gives a cystic adenomatoid malformation or a bronchogenic cyst — local, and often resectable. Prevented branching gives pulmonary hypoplasia, and the causes are all mechanical: a diaphragmatic hernia with gut in the chest, or oligohydramnios from renal agenesis. Remember which one is the killer. In Potter sequence the kidneys are the diagnosis but the lungs are the cause of death.

Beat 3 authors PEEL_LAYER outward on the organ layer to lift the mesenchymal coat off the epithelial tube. The current renderer degrades it to hiding structures tagged with that layer; the op is authored because layer removal is exactly how an epithelial-mesenchymal interaction should be shown.

'Alveolar development' is NOT claimed in covers[]. The alveolar stage appears here only as the fourth item on the timeline; the pneumocytes, surfactant, its composition and timing, and respiratory distress syndrome belong to that entry and are authored there.
'Respiratory diverticulum' is NOT claimed. The bronchial buds are the starting point of this scene, not its subject.
'Tracheoesophageal septum' is NOT claimed. Separation from the oesophagus and the fistula types belong to that entry.

Stage week boundaries are the standard teaching approximations and texts differ by one to two weeks, most often at the pseudoglandular/canalicular boundary (16 vs 17 weeks) and at the start of the alveolar stage (32, 36 weeks, or 'late fetal'). The narration uses the Langman/Moore figures that Nigerian MBBS papers mark against.

The left lung is given eight to ten bronchopulmonary segments because the apical and posterior segments of the upper lobe, and the anterior and medial basal segments of the lower lobe, commonly share a stem. Ten is often taught as the flat answer for both lungs; the range is stated so a student is not caught out either way.

Alveolar counts (about 50 million at term, about 300 million in the adult) vary widely between sources; they are given as orders of magnitude to make the point that most alveolarisation is postnatal, and the narration should not be read as quoting a measured figure.
